entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Theodosian Dynasty (379-457 CE) was the last ruling house of the unified Roman Empire, encompassing three emperors — Theodosius I (the Great), Arcadius, and Honorius (dividing the empire between east and west) — and culminating in Theodosius II and Valentinian III. This dynasty presided over the definitive Christianization of the Roman Empire (Theodosius I made Christianity the official state religion in 380 CE), the formal and permanent East-West division of the empire (395 CE), and the catastrophic fall of the Western Roman Empire (455-476 CE).

Theodosius I (r. 379-395 CE) was the last emperor to rule a unified Roman Empire. His 380 CE Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos Populos) made Nicene Christianity the official state religion, declaring other forms of Christianity and paganism illegal — a watershed moment in European religious history that ended the Roman Empire's traditional religious pluralism and established Christian orthodoxy as the legally enforced norm. Theodosius closed the Olympic Games (393 CE), destroyed pagan temples, and fundamentally transformed Roman religion.

The 395 CE division of the empire between Theodosius's sons — Arcadius taking the East, Honorius the West — was intended as an administrative arrangement but proved permanent. The Theodosian dynasty's western line watched helplessly as the Western Empire was dismembered by Visigoths (sack of Rome 410 CE), Vandals, Huns, and Germanic generals. The 410 sack of Rome under Honorius's reign was psychologically devastating to the Roman world — Saint Augustine wrote City of God partly in response. By 476 CE, the western dynasty had effectively ended.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Theodosian Dynasty — last rulers of a unified Rome, makers of Christianity the official Roman religion (380 CE), presiders over the permanent East-West division (395 CE), and witnesses of Rome's 410 CE sack — is one of the most historically pivotal dynasties in Western civilization, overseeing the transformation from pagan Rome to Christian Europe.
